words.shortDefinition: An explicit boundary within which a domain model is defined, internally consistent, and a single ubiquitous language applies.
words.simpleDefinition: A bounded context is a hard linguistic and model boundary drawn around one cohesive part of a system. Inside it every term has a precise, agreed meaning and the model is self-consistent. Outside it the same word may mean something entirely different. The boundary is what lets large systems stay coherent — each piece of the system owns its own model rather than sharing one sprawling global one.
words.longDefinition: Eric Evans introduced the bounded context in Part IV of Domain-Driven Design (2003) as the answer to a specific failure mode: multiple teams working on one codebase each develop their own informal model, the models collide, and the shared code becomes ambiguous. A bounded context makes the scope of a model explicit and enforced. Inside the boundary the team maintains a ubiquitous language — terms used identically in code, meetings, and documentation. The word 'Customer' in a Billing context has billing address, payment methods, and invoice history; in a Support context it has tickets, sentiment score, and communication preferences. They share a customer identifier but are genuinely different objects serving different purposes. A well-drawn bounded context contains a domain model, a ubiquitous language, a defined interface to the outside world, and an owning team. Vaughn Vernon's Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) opens with strategic design deliberately — a course correction after years of teams jumping to tactical patterns without establishing boundaries first.
words.connector: Think of a bounded context like a country with its own official language — inside its borders, words mean what the government says they mean; cross the border and the same words may have entirely different meanings or carry no authority at all.
words.techContext: After we split our monolith into a Billing bounded context and a Fulfilment bounded context, each team could evolve their model independently — adding billing-specific fields to 'Customer' without breaking the Fulfilment team's data structures.
words.exampleSentence: Drawing an explicit bounded context around the pricing engine allowed the team to rename 'rate' to 'tariff' in their model without touching the ten other services that used the word 'rate' to mean something else.
words.etymology: Evans borrowed 'context' from linguistics — the setting that determines the meaning of a word — and 'bounded' to signal that the boundary is explicit and enforced, not informal.

words.shortDefinition: The shared vocabulary built by engineers and domain experts that is used identically in code, conversations, and documentation.
words.simpleDefinition: Ubiquitous language is the disciplined practice of ensuring that domain experts and developers use the exact same words for the same concepts — and that those words appear unchanged as class names, method names, and event names in the code. When the expert says 'a policy lapses', the code has a method called 'lapse()' on a class called 'Policy'. No translation layer exists because no translation is needed.
words.longDefinition: Evans's most actionable insight in Domain-Driven Design is that miscommunication between domain experts and developers is not a cultural problem — it is a vocabulary problem with a technical solution. Ubiquitous language is not a glossary document; it is the living vocabulary enforced by both conversation and code. When the code uses different words than domain experts — when the expert says 'reservation' and the code says 'booking' — every conversation introduces a mapping step. That mapping step is where bugs are born. Ubiquitous language resolves this by mandating that the team pick one precise term and use it everywhere: in stand-ups, in design docs, in acceptance criteria, in class names, in method names, in event names. The language is also bounded: it applies within one bounded context. 'Account' means something precise in Banking and something different in Identity. The bounded context is the scope of the language's validity. Critically, the language must evolve with the domain. When domain experts rename a concept, the code renames it too. A ubiquitous language that exists in a document but not in the code is not ubiquitous — it is aspirational.
words.connector: Think of ubiquitous language like a contract between the business and the engineering team — the terms on the contract are the same terms in the code, so there is never a dispute about what was actually agreed.
words.techContext: After we established 'Shipment' (not 'Delivery' or 'Package') as the ubiquitous language term for our fulfilment context, every class, method, and Slack message used the same word — and the two-day onboarding confusion new engineers experienced dropped to almost nothing.
words.exampleSentence: The bug trace led back to a translation error — the domain expert said 'lapse' but the developer heard 'cancel', and the code used 'terminate', so three different things happened when one thing was intended.
words.etymology: From Latin ubique ('everywhere') — Evans chose the word deliberately to signal that the language must appear everywhere: in conversation, documentation, and code, with no exceptions.

words.shortDefinition: A cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with one root enforcing all invariants.
words.simpleDefinition: An aggregate is a consistency boundary drawn around a set of related domain objects — entities and value objects — that must always satisfy a shared set of business rules together. One designated entity, the aggregate root, is the only entry point for all changes. Code outside the aggregate can only hold a reference to the root, never to interior objects. All mutations flow through root methods, which check that every invariant is still satisfied before saving.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the aggregate pattern in Domain-Driven Design (2003) to answer: in a domain model with dozens of interrelated objects, how do you know what belongs together and what rules must hold at all times? The aggregate is the answer — a cluster of objects with a shared consistency guarantee and a single gatekeeper entity called the root. The root's three responsibilities are: entry point for all mutations (no external code touches interior entities directly), invariant enforcer (after any change, all cross-entity rules are checked), and identity anchor (the root's ID is how the aggregate is addressed). Vaughn Vernon's Effective Aggregate Design (2012) adds four practical rules: model true invariants in the aggregate, design small aggregates, reference other aggregates by identity only, and use eventual consistency outside the aggregate boundary. Large aggregates produce lock contention, memory pressure, and invariant ambiguity. Small aggregates are easier to load, test, and reason about. When two objects never appear in the same invariant together, they belong in separate aggregates connected by eventual consistency.
words.connector: Think of an aggregate like a department in a company — the department head (root) is the only door for external requests, and the department's internal rules (invariants) are the department head's responsibility to enforce before any decision is committed.
words.techContext: Designing the Order aggregate required us to include OrderLine entities (because the 'total quantity must not exceed allocation' invariant spans both) but hold only a CustomerId reference to the Customer aggregate, since no Order-level invariant involves Customer internals.
words.exampleSentence: When we put both Order and Inventory in a single transaction to 'be safe', we violated the aggregate boundary and created lock contention; splitting them into separate aggregates coordinated by a domain event resolved both problems.
words.etymology: From Latin aggregare ('to add to the flock') — individual objects are added to a single cluster that behaves as one unit for the purpose of consistency.

words.shortDefinition: An immutable domain object defined entirely by its attribute values, with no identity of its own.
words.simpleDefinition: A value object describes a domain concept whose entire meaning comes from its attribute values, not from a unique identifier. Two Money objects representing 50 USD are completely interchangeable — there is no 'first one' and 'second one'. Because they carry no identity, value objects are made immutable: instead of changing one, you create a new one with the new values. This immutability makes them safe to share, cache, and pass freely without defensive copying.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the value object alongside the entity in Chapter 5 of Domain-Driven Design as one of the two primary building blocks of a domain model. The distinction is identity: entities have identity that persists through state changes (a Customer is the same customer even after a name change); value objects have no meaningful identity beyond their attributes (two $50.00 USD Money values are indistinguishable and interchangeable). Classic examples include Money (amount + currency), DateRange (start + end), Coordinate (latitude + longitude), and EmailAddress. The immutability rule is the operational consequence of having no identity: since you cannot say which instance is 'the right one', you must never mutate one in place — callers would see unexpected changes to shared references. Instead, operations on value objects return new instances. This 'side-effect-free' behavior makes value objects safe for caching, equality comparison, and concurrent use. Primitive Obsession — using raw strings and integers for domain concepts instead of value objects — is the anti-pattern Evans warns against most directly: a raw string carries no domain validation and no domain behavior, while an EmailAddress value object validates its format on construction and can expose domain-meaningful operations.
words.connector: Think of value objects like dollar bills — you do not care which physical bill you have as long as it is a valid $50 bill; the identity of the particular piece of paper is irrelevant, only its face value matters.
words.techContext: Replacing our raw String email fields with an EmailAddress value object caught malformed addresses at construction time rather than at send time, and made the type system self-documenting: any function that takes EmailAddress cannot accidentally receive a username.
words.exampleSentence: After introducing Money as a value object rather than a bare Double, the compiler caught every place where we accidentally subtracted EUR amounts from USD amounts — the type system encoded the domain rule.
words.etymology: Evans coined the term to contrast with 'entity' — an object that carries 'value' (meaning from its attributes alone) rather than a persistent 'identity' (a tracked database row).

words.shortDefinition: A collection-like abstraction over persistence that provides retrieval and storage for aggregate roots only.
words.simpleDefinition: A repository gives domain code the illusion that aggregate roots live in an in-memory collection. From the caller's perspective you 'add' an order, 'get' it by ID, or query by criteria — you never write SQL, open sessions, or manage transactions. The repository interface belongs to the domain layer and speaks the ubiquitous language; the implementation that talks to Postgres or DynamoDB lives in the infrastructure layer and is swapped behind the interface.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the Repository pattern in Domain-Driven Design (2003) as the bridge between the pure domain model and persistence infrastructure. The defining metaphor is a collection: a repository behaves like a Set of aggregate roots that survives process restart. Two responsibilities: hiding the mechanics of persistence (SQL, ORM sessions, connection pools, caches are all invisible to the domain), and speaking the domain language (method names like findActiveOrdersForCustomer() express business intent, not storage operations). The one-to-one rule is structural: each repository corresponds to exactly one aggregate root. There is an OrderRepository and a CustomerRepository — but no OrderLineRepository, because OrderLine has no meaningful existence outside its Order aggregate. Creating a repository for an interior entity is a design smell that signals the aggregate boundary was drawn incorrectly. The repository interface is declared in the domain layer; implementations live in the infrastructure layer. This inversion of control is what makes unit testing domain logic fast: test doubles substitute an in-memory repository without touching a database. Evans also distinguishes repositories from DAOs (Data Access Objects): a DAO speaks database rows; a repository speaks aggregate objects. The distinction matters because a DAO-heavy codebase typically produces an anemic domain model where domain logic leaks into service layers to work around the row-based abstraction.
words.connector: Think of a repository like a library card catalogue — you look up a book by its attributes or ID, and the catalogue handles whether to fetch it from the stacks, the archive, or a branch library. You never need to know the retrieval mechanism.
words.techContext: Declaring OrderRepository as a protocol in the domain module let us run the full suite of domain logic tests against an InMemoryOrderRepository in under a second, while the production PostgresOrderRepository ran only in integration tests.
words.exampleSentence: The repository interface hid five different storage strategies — hot cache, warm cache, primary Postgres, replica, and archive — behind a single findByOrderId() method that the domain layer called without knowing which tier responded.
words.etymology: From Latin repositorium ('a place where things are stored'); Evans borrowed the term to signal a storage abstraction that holds domain objects, not raw data rows.

words.shortDefinition: A stateless operation that belongs to the domain but does not fit naturally on any single entity or value object.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain service is the right home for a domain operation that is meaningful to business experts but cannot be naturally placed on any single entity or value object without making that object bloated or awkwardly responsible. It is stateless — all information needed is passed as arguments, nothing is stored between calls — and it is written in the ubiquitous language. It is NOT a place to dump logic that nobody else wanted.
words.longDefinition: Evans identified three criteria for a domain service in Domain-Driven Design (2003): the operation is domain-significant (domain experts name and discuss it); it is stateless (nothing is stored on the service instance between calls); and it does not fit naturally on an entity or value object (placing it there would make the entity bloated or give it an awkward responsibility). A canonical example is a currency conversion service that takes a Money value in one currency, a ConversionRate value object, and returns a Money value in a target currency. Neither the Money value object nor the ConversionRate knows the other's responsibilities — a domain service is the natural fit. Domain services differ critically from application services: a domain service contains pure business logic and can be called from within the domain layer; an application service orchestrates a use case — it loads aggregates via repositories, calls domain methods, publishes events, and commits transactions — but contains no business logic of its own. Domain services are also distinct from infrastructure services, which implement technical capabilities (email delivery, database access, HTTP) that the domain model depends on via interfaces. The most common abuse of domain services is using them as an escape hatch for logic that really belongs on an entity — producing the anemic domain model anti-pattern where entities are bags of getters and every 'service' does the real work.
words.connector: Think of a domain service like a specialist brought in for a specific procedure — neither the patient (entity) nor the instrument (value object) performs the surgery alone, but the specialist's skill is the domain operation that requires all three together.
words.techContext: Our FundsTransferService is a domain service — it takes two Account aggregates and a Money amount, validates cross-account business rules, and returns two modified accounts. Neither Account could own this logic without becoming aware of the other.
words.exampleSentence: We tried putting transferFunds() on the Account entity, but Account would have needed to load the target Account to check its rules — a clear sign the operation belonged in a domain service, not on the entity.
words.etymology: Evans borrowed 'service' from enterprise architecture patterns but qualified it with 'domain' to distinguish operations that carry business meaning from infrastructure or application coordination services.

words.shortDefinition: A thin orchestration layer that coordinates domain objects to fulfill a use case without containing business logic.
words.simpleDefinition: An application service is the choreographer of a use case. It loads aggregates from repositories, calls domain methods that contain the business logic, publishes domain events, and commits the transaction. It contains no business rules of its own — it is the glue between the delivery mechanism (HTTP, queue, CLI) and the domain model. Keeping application services thin is the clearest indicator that business logic is living where it belongs, inside the domain.
words.longDefinition: Application services sit at the intersection of the delivery mechanism and the domain model. In a layered architecture they occupy the application layer; in hexagonal architecture they are driven by a primary port adapter. Their responsibilities are purely orchestrational: receive a command or query, authenticate and authorize if required, load the relevant aggregate root(s) via repositories, call domain methods on those aggregates to perform the business operation, collect any domain events raised during the operation, save the aggregate back to its repository, publish events to the event bus, and return a response to the caller. A thick application service — one that contains if-else chains encoding business rules, calculates prices, or decides whether an operation is allowed — is a warning sign: the business logic has leaked out of the domain model into an orchestration layer. The test for whether logic belongs in an application service or a domain service is simple: could a business expert read this code and recognize it as a business rule? If yes, it belongs in the domain. If it is plumbing — 'get this, call that, save the result' — it belongs in the application service.
words.connector: Think of an application service like a stage director — it tells each actor (domain object) when to enter and what scene to play, but it does not perform any of the roles itself. The acting (business logic) belongs to the actors.
words.techContext: Our PlaceOrderApplicationService is 15 lines: load the cart, call cart.checkout(), save the resulting order, publish OrderPlaced. All business rules live in Cart and Order — the application service is deliberately dumb.
words.exampleSentence: When the application service grew to 80 lines with discount calculations and eligibility checks embedded in it, we knew the domain model had gone anemic — those rules belonged on the Order aggregate, not in the orchestration layer.
words.etymology: Evans used 'application' to mean 'the application of domain logic to a specific use case' — distinguishing this orchestration layer from the domain logic layer it coordinates.

words.shortDefinition: The part of the domain that provides unique competitive advantage — where DDD's deepest investment is directed.
words.simpleDefinition: The core subdomain is what makes your business genuinely different from competitors — the capability they cannot easily replicate because it is built on proprietary knowledge, unique data, or hard-won expertise. It is where you assign your best engineers, apply DDD's full tactical toolbox, and iterate the model continuously with domain experts. Outsourcing or simplifying the core subdomain means outsourcing your competitive advantage.
words.longDefinition: Vernon's Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) opens with the subdomain classification because it is the first strategic decision: before you can decide how to model something, you must decide how much to invest in modeling it. The core subdomain is the answer to 'where does maximum investment pay off?' Its defining properties: competitors cannot easily replicate it (it is proprietary knowledge or unique data); it changes frequently as the business learns (a stable subdomain is a sign it has matured into something generic); domain experts actively care about its correctness (if nobody can articulate what makes it special, it probably is not core); and it should never be outsourced or bought off-the-shelf (buying a core subdomain means buying a competitor's version of your differentiator). In a ride-sharing company, driver-matching algorithms and dynamic pricing are core. In a bank, the credit risk model is core. In a healthcare analytics company, the clinical decision support engine is core. The correct investment posture for the core subdomain is DDD's full tactical arsenal: aggregates, domain events, elaborate value objects, continuous collaboration with domain experts, and a willingness to accept higher local complexity in exchange for modeling precision.
words.connector: Think of the core subdomain like the secret recipe in a restaurant — you never outsource recipe development to a catering company, you never reveal it to a supplier, and you hire the best chefs to refine it continuously.
words.techContext: Identifying credit risk scoring as our core subdomain — rather than letting it live as a few fields in a general-purpose Loan entity — justified a dedicated bounded context, a senior team, and six months of model refinement with actuaries.
words.exampleSentence: When the team proposed using a third-party algorithmic trading library for the investment recommendation engine, the CTO rejected it on strategic grounds: that was the core subdomain, the thing customers paid for, and it could not be outsourced.
words.etymology: Evans coined the subdomain classification in Domain-Driven Design; Vernon made the core/supporting/generic trichotomy explicit in IDDD as a framework for investment decisions.

words.shortDefinition: A necessary but non-differentiating part of the domain that may be built in-house but at a lower investment tier.
words.simpleDefinition: A supporting subdomain is necessary for the business to operate but provides no competitive advantage. It is too specific to your business for an off-the-shelf product to fit perfectly, but it is not the reason customers choose you. You build it in-house for control reasons, but you do not over-engineer it — you staff it with mid-level engineers, accept simpler design patterns, and reserve DDD's full tactical investment for the core.
words.longDefinition: Vernon's subdomain trichotomy places the supporting subdomain in the middle tier: custom enough that vendor solutions do not fit exactly, but stable enough and undifferentiated enough that deep modeling investment would be misallocated. A delivery company's driver onboarding workflow is supporting: it requires domain knowledge (employment contracts, vehicle inspection rules, regulatory compliance) that a generic HR SaaS does not handle, but no customer chooses the delivery company because of onboarding excellence. Distinguishing features: the domain is moderately stable (not the frontier of business innovation); an off-the-shelf solution would require too much customization to be viable; and correct implementation requires domain understanding but not the deepest available expertise. The build decision is defensible for supporting subdomains when vendor lock-in risk is high, integration cost is prohibitive, or the subdomain may eventually migrate toward core as the business evolves. The design posture: simpler patterns are acceptable (CRUD is often fine), mid-level engineers are appropriate, and the bar for complexity justification is higher. A common error is treating too many subdomains as core and applying expensive DDD patterns uniformly — the supporting subdomain classification is what prevents that waste.
words.connector: Think of a supporting subdomain like the kitchen prep work in a restaurant — absolutely necessary for the meal to happen, requiring real skill, but not what earns the Michelin star. You need good cooks for prep, but your executive chef focuses on the signature dishes.
words.techContext: We classified our driver onboarding workflow as a supporting subdomain — built in-house because generic HR tools could not handle vehicle class rules, but modeled with CRUD rather than full DDD patterns, freeing the senior team for route optimization.
words.exampleSentence: Recognising reporting as a supporting subdomain rather than core allowed the team to ship it in three weeks with a simple CRUD design, instead of spending two months applying the same modeling depth as the fraud detection engine.
words.etymology: Evans established the subdomain classification in Domain-Driven Design; Vernon articulated the three-tier investment framework explicitly in IDDD Chapter 2 to give teams a principled basis for resource allocation.

words.shortDefinition: A solved-problem domain area best served by buying off-the-shelf and integrating behind an abstraction.
words.simpleDefinition: A generic subdomain is a business capability that virtually every company needs and that the market has already solved well — authentication, payments, email delivery, search, CMS. The canonical answer is: buy a best-of-breed solution and integrate it behind an abstraction so your domain model never directly speaks the vendor's language. Building a generic subdomain from scratch wastes engineering time that should go toward the core.
words.longDefinition: Evans included the generic subdomain in Domain-Driven Design as the third tier of the problem-space classification, and Vernon's IDDD makes the investment logic explicit. Generic subdomains exist in virtually every business: authentication (Auth0, Okta), accounting (QuickBooks, Xero), full-text search (Elasticsearch, Algolia), email delivery (SendGrid), and content management (Contentful). Building any of these from scratch consumes engineering capacity and incurs ongoing maintenance cost without producing competitive advantage. The canonical answer: buy best-of-breed and integrate behind an abstraction. The abstraction matters critically. If the vendor's model bleeds into your domain model — if you have Stripe Customer objects mixed with your own Customer entities — you have coupled your domain model to vendor internals. When you switch vendors, the coupling propagates through your codebase. An Anti-Corruption Layer isolates the translation. The common trap: teams build custom authentication or payment systems because 'the integration looked complex.' The complexity of integrating Stripe is far lower than the complexity of maintaining PCI DSS compliance on homegrown payment infrastructure. Generic subdomains are the first place to look when deciding what not to build.
words.connector: Think of a generic subdomain like the electricity in a restaurant — vital infrastructure that every business needs, but nobody opens a restaurant because they built better wiring. You buy from the utility company and focus on the food.
words.techContext: We classified authentication as a generic subdomain, integrated Auth0 behind an IdentityService interface, and freed the three engineers who were maintaining a homegrown JWT implementation to work on the recommender system instead.
words.exampleSentence: After classifying the notification system as a generic subdomain and switching to SendGrid behind a thin NotificationPort interface, we removed 8,000 lines of homegrown SMTP infrastructure that had been breaking in production every few weeks.
words.etymology: Evans used 'generic' in the sense of 'not specific to this business' — a commodity capability that the market supplies rather than one that the organization must create.

words.shortDefinition: A domain pattern that encapsulates complex creation logic for aggregates or entities, keeping constructors clean.
words.simpleDefinition: A factory is a dedicated object or method that knows how to construct a valid aggregate or entity from parts, applying all the business rules that govern its creation. When constructing an aggregate is complex — requiring multiple collaborators, validation across several invariants, or transformation of raw inputs — a factory extracts that complexity from the root's constructor and makes creation intent explicit in the domain language.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the Factory as a domain pattern in Domain-Driven Design (2003, Chapter 6), adapting the GoF Factory pattern specifically for the domain model context. The problem it solves: aggregate constructors that must validate complex invariants, assemble nested entities and value objects, enforce business rules about initial state, or accept inputs in non-domain formats become unreadable and test-hostile. A factory extracts this logic into a dedicated creation context. Two factory forms appear in DDD codebases: factory methods on the aggregate root itself (Order.createFrom(cart:) is a natural fit when the factory logic is small and the aggregate is the appropriate home), and standalone factory objects (CartCheckoutFactory) when the creation process is elaborate, requires dependencies, or coordinates multiple aggregates. The factory speaks the ubiquitous language: a PolicyFactory.issue(application:, riskAssessment:) method uses the same words an underwriter uses, making the creation intent clear to both engineers and domain experts. The key distinction from a simple constructor: a factory is responsible for producing a valid, fully-formed aggregate that satisfies all creation invariants; a constructor that does the same work at scale produces an object-graph-building mess that obscures the domain concept behind structural plumbing.
words.connector: Think of a factory like a master baker who knows the recipe for creating a specific type of cake — the customer states 'I want a wedding cake with these specifications' and the baker handles all the steps to produce a valid finished product.
words.techContext: We extracted InsurancePolicy creation into a PolicyFactory.issue() method because the constructor had grown to 14 parameters and contained 200 lines of underwriting eligibility checks — the factory made the business intent legible again.
words.exampleSentence: Moving loan application validation from the LoanAccount constructor into a LoanFactory.open() factory method reduced the constructor to six lines and gave the creation process a name the loan officers actually recognized.
words.etymology: Adapted from the GoF Factory design pattern (1994); Evans contextualised it for domain modeling, emphasising that the factory produces domain-valid objects rather than arbitrary objects.

words.shortDefinition: A business rule encapsulated as an object that can be combined, queried, and passed independently of entities.
words.simpleDefinition: A specification wraps a single business rule — 'customer is eligible for premium tier', 'order qualifies for free shipping' — in a named, testable object with an isSatisfiedBy(candidate) method. Specifications can be composed with AND, OR, and NOT combinators to build complex rules from simple reusable predicates without tangling the logic inside entities or services.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the Specification pattern in Domain-Driven Design (2003, Chapter 9) as a solution to three problems: validation (is this object valid for an operation?), selection (which objects in a collection match a rule?), and creation-to-order (build an object satisfying these criteria). The pattern encapsulates each business rule as an independent, named object. A single specification is a predicate — it has an isSatisfiedBy(T) method that returns true or false. Evans and Fowler's earlier work on the pattern showed that specifications become especially powerful when composed: PremiumEligible.and(not(HasOutstandingBalance)) reads almost like a business policy statement. In a DDD repository context, a specification passed to the repository's find method lets the repository translate it to a database predicate while keeping the domain layer free of SQL. In Evans's book the repository chapter demonstrates exactly this: the CalendarPeriod specification passed to ShiftRepository.findShifts(satisfying:) allows the repository to generate the appropriate WHERE clause without the domain knowing the persistence technology. The specification pattern is particularly valuable when business rules are volatile — when eligibility rules change monthly, an isolated specification object is far cheaper to change and test than rules tangled inside aggregate methods or service layers.
words.connector: Think of specifications like checklist templates in hiring — each criterion (must have 5 years experience, must have security clearance) is a separate checkable item that you can combine into a full candidate profile filter without rewriting the evaluation logic each time.
words.techContext: Our PromotionEligibilitySpecification encapsulates the six conditions for discount eligibility; passing it to OrderRepository.findEligible() lets the repository generate the SQL while the domain owns the business rule.
words.exampleSentence: When the eligibility rules for premium membership changed for the fourth time in two quarters, having them encapsulated in a PremiumEligibilitySpecification meant the change was a one-line predicate swap instead of a hunt through four services.
words.etymology: Evans and Fowler developed the Specification pattern together; the name reflects that the object 'specifies' a criterion rather than executing behavior on the candidate directly.

words.shortDefinition: The observation that system architecture mirrors the communication structure of the teams that build it.
words.simpleDefinition: Conway's Law says that the software you build will naturally take the shape of your organisation — not your architecture diagrams, not your design principles, but your actual team communication structure. If three teams own one system, the system will have three implicit subsystems at the seams of team interaction. In DDD terms, bounded context boundaries and team ownership boundaries tend to align whether you plan them to or not.
words.longDefinition: Melvin Conway observed in 1967 that 'organisations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organisations.' In DDD terms, bounded context boundaries and team communication structures are deeply linked. A bounded context without a clear team owner decays — multiple teams writing to the same bounded context each introduce their own terms, blurring the ubiquitous language. A team split across two bounded contexts creates friction — the seam between contexts becomes underdefined because it is a seam within the team's own cognition. Conversely, when a team restructures, the bounded contexts it owned become contested or orphaned, which is a leading indicator of model degradation. The practical implication: when drawing bounded context boundaries, look at the team topology. If the context map and the org chart are radically misaligned, you have either the wrong context map or the wrong org chart. Vernon explicitly links team ownership to bounded contexts in IDDD: 'One team owns one bounded context. When multiple teams own a context, the context needs a shared kernel or political coordination to stay coherent.' Skelton and Pais's Team Topologies (2019) operationalises this relationship, making the stream-aligned team the pattern for bounded context ownership.
words.connector: Think of Conway's Law like how a relay race team runs — if two different training groups each own two legs of the race, the handoff between their respective runners will be the weakest point, no matter how good the individual runners are.
words.techContext: Our context map showed a Payments context straddling two teams. Conway's Law predicted — correctly — that the seam within Payments was the system's most frequent source of integration failures, resolved only after we aligned team ownership with context boundaries.
words.exampleSentence: Conway's Law predicted our problem before we diagnosed it: the monolith's three most buggy modules exactly mapped to the three teams that had historically owned overlapping parts of the codebase.
words.etymology: Named for Melvin Conway, who published the observation in 'How Do Committees Invent?' in Datamation magazine in April 1968; Fred Brooks popularised it in The Mythical Man-Month (1975).

words.shortDefinition: The strategy of restructuring teams to match the desired architecture so that Conway's Law works in your favor.
words.simpleDefinition: The Inverse Conway Manoeuvre flips Conway's Law from a warning into a design tool. Instead of letting team structure accidentally determine architecture, you first design the architecture — draw the bounded context map — and then restructure teams to align with it. Conway's Law will then produce the system shape you intended rather than one determined by historical accident.
words.longDefinition: The Inverse Conway Manoeuvre was named and popularised by Skelton and Pais in Team Topologies (2019) but the concept appeared earlier in the microservices and DDD communities. The insight is that Conway's Law is bidirectional: just as team structure produces system structure, intentionally designing team structure to match a desired system architecture will cause the system to evolve toward that architecture organically. In DDD practice, this means: draw the context map first, with the correct bounded context boundaries — the ones that align with domain subdomains and provide clean model isolation. Then reorganise the teams so each bounded context has one owning team. Conway's Law now works in your favor: the team structure reinforces the context boundary because each team's natural communication is within its own context, not across contexts. Importantly, the manoeuvre requires organisational authority — engineering leadership and product management must align on the team restructuring. Without that authority, the team structure drifts back to its previous shape. Skelton and Pais pair the manoeuvre with specific team interaction modes: stream-aligned teams for core context ownership, platform teams for shared infrastructure, and enabling teams for temporary capability uplift.
words.connector: Think of the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre like urban planning for organisational design — instead of observing where the footpaths naturally form and paving them (Conway's Law), you plan where you want paths to go and build the environment that makes people naturally walk there.
words.techContext: After drawing our target context map with four distinct bounded contexts, engineering and product jointly reorganised six mixed-function squads into four stream-aligned teams, each owning one context — within two quarters the inter-team integration issues that had consumed 30% of sprint time dropped to near zero.
words.exampleSentence: Rather than waiting for the microservices architecture to emerge organically, the CTO applied the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre — aligning team charters with the target context map before writing a single line of the new system.
words.etymology: Named 'Inverse' because it inverts the direction of causality in Conway's Law — instead of team structure producing system structure passively, you deliberately design team structure to produce a chosen system structure; popularised in Team Topologies (Skelton & Pais, 2019).

words.shortDefinition: A system-level diagram showing every bounded context and the explicit integration relationships between them.
words.simpleDefinition: A context map is the honest, system-wide picture of every bounded context and how each one relates to every other. It names every integration pattern in use — Anti-Corruption Layer, Open Host Service, Conformist — and shows which direction model changes flow. It documents reality as it is, including legacy systems and awkward seams, not as it ideally should be.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the context map in Chapter 14 of Domain-Driven Design as the antidote to navigating a large multi-context system by folklore. Without an explicit map, integration patterns accumulate silently: one team calls another's endpoint without a clear contract, a downstream team copies an upstream model and the copies drift, a third team rewrites a service and breaks unknown consumers. A context map makes all of this explicit. It shows every bounded context as a named box (including third-party systems, legacy systems, and external vendors), every integration as a labeled relationship line, and the upstream/downstream direction of every relationship. The labeled relationship patterns carry real design information: a Conformist label means the downstream adopts the upstream's model without translation — a deliberate decision with known maintenance consequences. An ACL label means the downstream protects itself with a translation boundary. A Shared Kernel label signals co-owned code that requires governance. A context map should document reality, not aspiration. Showing legacy systems accurately, including their integration debts, is what makes the map useful as a refactoring guide. Vernon's guidance: start by mapping what exists, then use the map to drive incremental improvement toward better-drawn boundaries and healthier integration patterns.
words.connector: Think of a context map like a political map of a continent — it shows which territories exist, who owns what border, which countries have treaties with which others, and where the disputed regions are. Without the map, every diplomatic interaction happens in ignorance of the broader landscape.
words.techContext: Drawing our first context map revealed that six services were all conformist consumers of the legacy Order Management System — a dependency nobody had documented, whose scheduled decommission would have broken half the platform without warning.
words.exampleSentence: The context map showed that our Payments context was both upstream to Billing (via an Open Host Service) and downstream to Order Management (as a Conformist) — an asymmetry the team had never articulated, which explained why Payments changes were never stable.

codeExample.code:
// Context map (ASCII — shows real integration patterns)

  [Order Mgmt] --ACL--> [Inventory]
       |                     |
  OHS+PL               Conformist
       |                     |
       v                     v
  [Payment (Stripe)]  [Shipping (3PL)]

Key:
  ACL       = Anti-Corruption Layer (Order translates Inventory model)
  OHS+PL    = Open Host Service + Published Language (stable versioned API)
  Conformist = Shipping adapter adopts Inventory address model unchanged

words.etymology: Evans coined 'context map' as a combination of 'context' (the bounded context) and 'map' (a spatial representation of relationships) — the term deliberately evokes navigation and geographic orientation.

words.shortDefinition: The directional relationship between contexts where the upstream model influences the downstream, and changes flow that way.
words.simpleDefinition: In a context map, the upstream bounded context is the one whose model sets the terms — its changes propagate to others. The downstream context is the one that must react to those changes. The upstream has power (it changes on its own schedule) and the downstream has dependency (it must adapt or protect itself). The asymmetry is important: the upstream is not automatically 'better' — it simply owns the authoritative model on that integration point.
words.longDefinition: Evans established the upstream/downstream vocabulary in Domain-Driven Design to make the power dynamics of context-map relationships explicit. When a change in Context A forces an adaptation in Context B, A is upstream and B is downstream. The upstream team controls its model on its own schedule; the downstream team absorbs or translates those changes. This asymmetry matters for architectural decisions: a downstream team that cannot influence the upstream's model must protect itself with an Anti-Corruption Layer or accept a Conformist relationship. The Customer-Supplier pattern is the negotiated middle ground: the upstream (supplier) agrees to consider the downstream (customer) team's needs when making changes, creating a collaborative rather than unilateral relationship. Shared Kernel involves both teams in every model change — the highest integration with the highest coordination cost. Partnership is the symmetric case where two teams co-evolve their contexts together. Understanding the upstream/downstream direction on each integration line is what allows a team to assess its dependency risk: a downstream context dependent on a Big Ball of Mud upstream has high vulnerability; a downstream context with an ACL has protection. The direction also determines who owns the translation burden in integration patterns.
words.connector: Think of upstream/downstream like a river-town relationship — a factory upstream can pollute the water, and the downstream towns must install filtration (an ACL) or accept whatever comes downstream (Conformist). The upstream town does not have to think about what it puts in the river unless a negotiated agreement forces it to.
words.techContext: Mapping our Payment context as downstream to the Identity context — rather than treating them as peers — clarified why Payment was always the one rewriting adapters when Identity changed its user model, and justified building an ACL.
words.exampleSentence: Once we labelled the Order context as upstream to the Notification context, the Notification team understood why their service kept breaking — they were conformist consumers of Order changes they had no influence over, and they needed an ACL.
words.etymology: Evans borrowed the upstream/downstream metaphor from hydrology — in a river, upstream is where things originate and changes flow from; downstream is where the consequences arrive. The metaphor captures the power asymmetry naturally.

words.shortDefinition: An anti-pattern of using raw primitives (String, int) for domain concepts instead of expressive value objects.
words.simpleDefinition: Primitive obsession is the habit of representing domain concepts as raw language primitives — a customer's email as a String, an order amount as a Double, a policy number as an Int — rather than wrapping them in value objects. The result is that business rules about those concepts live scattered across callers rather than encapsulated in the concept's type, making bugs easy to introduce and hard to find.
words.longDefinition: Evans identified primitive obsession as a symptom of an anemic domain model and a direct anti-pattern to the value object principle. When a developer stores an email address as a raw String, the type carries no domain information: it cannot validate format on assignment, cannot express that certain operations are only valid for email addresses, and cannot prevent passing a username where an email is expected. When an order total is a raw Double, floating-point arithmetic can silently lose cents, there is no currency attached, and nothing prevents subtracting EUR from USD. Replacing these primitives with value objects — EmailAddress, Money, PolicyNumber, Quantity — moves the domain rules into the type system where the compiler enforces them. This is the operational payoff of the value object principle: domain concepts described as rich types rather than bare primitives self-document their constraints, centralise their validation, and make illegal states unrepresentable in the type system. Primitive obsession is one of Martin Fowler's and Kent Beck's original code smells (Refactoring, 1999) and Evans incorporated it into the DDD value object discussion precisely because it is the most common reason teams fail to model domain concepts as first-class objects. The refactoring is straightforward: identify the concept, create a value object with a private raw backing field, move all validation and domain behaviour onto the value object, and update all call sites.
words.connector: Think of primitive obsession like labelling every jar in a kitchen 'stuff' — technically accurate, but you lose all the information you need to use them correctly, and swapping salt for sugar becomes something the type system cannot prevent.
words.techContext: Replacing the raw String customerId fields with a strongly typed CustomerID value object eliminated an entire class of bug where customer IDs were accidentally passed where product IDs were expected — the compiler now rejects the swap.
words.exampleSentence: The 'wrong currency' production incident traced back to primitive obsession — the exchange rate calculation mixed USD Doubles with EUR Doubles, and without a Money value object, the type system had no way to prevent it.
words.etymology: Coined by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler as one of the original code smells in Refactoring (1999); Evans incorporated it into Domain-Driven Design as a direct motivation for the value object pattern.

words.shortDefinition: The rule that entities are equal when their identities match, regardless of how their other attributes differ.
words.simpleDefinition: Identity equality is the equality rule for entities: two entity instances are the same entity if and only if they share the same identity (their unique ID), regardless of any differences in their other attributes. A Customer who changes their name, address, and email is still the same Customer — the identity persists through all state changes. This contrasts directly with value equality, which is how value objects compare.
words.longDefinition: Evans established identity equality as the definitional equality rule for entities in Domain-Driven Design (2003, Chapter 5). The principle reflects a fundamental business reality: many domain objects have continuity through time. A bank account is the same account even after its balance changes. An order is the same order even after its status transitions from Pending to Shipped to Delivered. A customer is the same customer even after a legal name change. What makes these objects 'the same' across changes is not their attribute values — it is a stable identity that persists through the object's entire lifecycle. In code, implementing identity equality means overriding equals() and hashCode() to compare only the identity field, not all fields. Two Customer objects with the same CustomerID are equal even if every other property differs — because they are two in-memory representations of the same real-world entity. Implementations that compare all fields (structural equality) on an entity produce subtle bugs: a cached entity with stale attribute values will not be found equal to a freshly loaded entity with the same ID, breaking collections, deduplication logic, and change detection. The identity field itself is typically a typed value object (CustomerId wrapping a UUID) rather than a raw primitive, combining identity equality with the benefits of strong typing.
words.connector: Think of identity equality like a passport — the same person is 'equal' to themselves across different photos, haircuts, weight changes, and even name changes, because the passport number (identity) is what uniquely identifies them, not their appearance.
words.techContext: When we switched our Customer equals() from full-field comparison to identity-only comparison, the duplicate-customer bug in our shopping cart disappeared — two sessions holding different versions of the same Customer now correctly resolved to the same entity.
words.exampleSentence: Identity equality caught the subtle bug where the search results page showed the same customer twice — one loaded from cache with a stale address, one fresh from the database — that structural equality had been treating as two different customers.
words.etymology: Evans borrowed 'identity' from philosophy of personal identity — the question of what makes a person the same person over time — and applied it to domain objects that persist and change through their lifecycle.

words.shortDefinition: The rule that value objects are equal when all their constituent attributes are equal, with no notion of identity.
words.simpleDefinition: Value equality is the equality rule for value objects: two instances are equal if and only if every one of their attribute values is equal. There is no 'identity' — no separate ID field to compare. Two Money objects both representing 50 USD are interchangeable and equal in every meaningful sense, regardless of which piece of memory they occupy. This is the direct complement to entity identity equality.
words.longDefinition: Evans established value equality as the definitional equality rule for value objects in Domain-Driven Design (2003, Chapter 5). Because value objects have no separate identity beyond their attributes, structural equality — comparing all attribute values — is the complete definition of sameness. Two instances of Money(50, .usd) are equivalent in every way that matters for the domain: they can substitute for each other freely, they produce the same results in any calculation, and caching or deduplicating them loses no information. Implementing value equality correctly means overriding equals() and hashCode() to compare all attribute fields. Omitting any field causes subtle bugs: a Money value that compares currency but not amount would declare 50 USD equal to 99 USD if both have currency USD. Value objects used as keys in sets or dictionaries depend on correct value equality — a wrong implementation breaks collection semantics. Value equality also drives the immutability requirement: if a value object were mutable, modifying one instance would change its 'value' and therefore its identity, which is incoherent. Immutability and value equality together make value objects safe to share, copy, and cache — any operation that needs a 'different' value produces a new instance rather than mutating the existing one. This property also enables safe multi-threading: immutable value objects require no locking.
words.connector: Think of value equality like comparing recipes — two recipe cards for chocolate chip cookies are 'the same recipe' if they list the same ingredients in the same amounts, regardless of which physical card you are holding. There is no card identity, only ingredient identity.
words.techContext: After implementing value equality on our DateRange value object, the deduplication step in our scheduling service correctly collapsed twenty identical DateRange instances from different parts of the system into one, eliminating the redundant calendar block creation.
words.exampleSentence: The bug in the discount engine was a missing field in the DiscountCode equality check — two codes with the same text but different expiry dates were being treated as equal because the hashCode only hashed the code string, not the expiry.
words.etymology: Evans used 'value' in the mathematical sense — a value is defined entirely by what it is, not by where it lives; two expressions with the same value are interchangeable, just as 2+2 and 4 are interchangeable.

words.shortDefinition: A method on a value object that returns a new value without mutating state, supporting safe composition.
words.simpleDefinition: Side-effect-free behavior describes methods on value objects that compute and return a new value rather than modifying existing state. Calling money.adding(tax) does not change money — it returns a new Money instance with the tax applied. Because no existing state is changed, these methods are safe to call anywhere, compose freely, test in isolation, and reason about without tracking hidden mutations.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced side-effect-free functions as a property of value objects in Domain-Driven Design (2003, Chapter 6), drawing on the functional programming principle that a function without side effects — one that depends only on its inputs and returns only its output — is predictable, composable, and safe. For domain modeling, this principle applies directly to value objects: since value objects are defined by their attributes (not by identity), and since they are immutable, all meaningful operations on them must produce new value objects rather than mutating existing ones. money.add(other) does not change money; it returns a new Money. dateRange.extending(by: days) does not change dateRange; it returns a new DateRange. The benefits compound: operations can be chained without worrying about intermediate state leaking. Tests need no setup to ensure a clean initial state. Concurrent callers cannot interfere with each other through shared mutable state. The method's behavior is fully determined by its inputs alone, making it testable with simple parameterised examples. Evans contrasts this with commands — operations that change state and return nothing meaningful — which belong on entities and aggregate roots. Value objects express computation; entities and aggregates express state transitions. Keeping these concerns separated makes the model's intent legible: a value object method computes a new descriptive state; an entity method performs a business action.
words.connector: Think of side-effect-free behavior like a recipe instruction: 'combine these ingredients to produce this result' — the ingredients are not consumed or changed by the description, and you can read the recipe a thousand times without affecting any kitchen.
words.techContext: Implementing DateRange.splitting(at:) as a side-effect-free method that returns two new DateRange values allowed our scheduling service to compose complex date operations in a pipeline without defensive copying between each step.
words.exampleSentence: Expressing all temperature conversion operations as side-effect-free methods on a Temperature value object meant the weather service could chain a dozen conversions in a data pipeline without any intermediate mutation risks.
words.etymology: Evans borrowed 'side-effect-free' from functional programming, where a function without side effects is called 'pure' — it depends only on its arguments and affects only its return value, with no observable effect on the external world.

words.shortDefinition: The guarantee that all invariants within an aggregate boundary are satisfied within a single database transaction.
words.simpleDefinition: Transactional consistency is the strong consistency guarantee that applies inside a single aggregate: all of its invariants are enforced atomically within one database transaction. If any invariant is violated, the entire transaction rolls back. This is the consistency model used for changes within an aggregate boundary — cross-aggregate consistency uses eventual consistency instead.
words.longDefinition: Evans established the aggregate as the transactional unit in Domain-Driven Design (2003): changes to an aggregate's root and all its interior entities are committed as one atomic unit. Vernon's Effective Aggregate Design formalises this as the one-aggregate-per-transaction rule: modify exactly one aggregate per transaction. The rule is not a performance hint — it is the structural guarantee that aggregates are self-contained consistency units. When a transaction spans multiple aggregates, those aggregates become implicitly coupled: their invariants now depend on each other's state within the transaction, undermining the decomposition. Transactional consistency within an aggregate provides three guarantees that are fundamental to domain modeling: all-or-nothing (either every invariant holds after the transaction or none of the changes are visible), isolation (concurrent transactions cannot observe partial states of another aggregate's modification), and durability (once committed, the invariant-satisfying state persists through failure). These guarantees are what make the aggregate a reliable building block: callers can assume that any aggregate retrieved from a repository satisfies all its invariants, because the repository only ever saved aggregates in valid states. Cross-aggregate consistency does not carry these guarantees — it is eventual — but within the aggregate boundary, the transaction provides the full consistency model that business rules require.
words.connector: Think of transactional consistency like a legal contract — all clauses must be satisfied at the moment of signing or none of the obligations are binding. The aggregate is the scope of the contract, and the transaction is the signing moment.
words.techContext: Because the 'an order must have at least one line to be confirmed' invariant spans Order and its OrderLine entities, both are inside the same aggregate — the transaction that commits an Order confirmation atomically validates both the root and all interior entities.
words.exampleSentence: The concurrency bug appeared because two services were updating the same Order aggregate in overlapping transactions; each checked the quantity invariant against a version without the other's changes, and both succeeded, producing a quantity that violated the rule.
words.etymology: From Latin transactio ('a carrying through to completion') + consistere ('to stand firm together') — a transaction is an operation carried through to completion only when all its parts stand firm together.

words.shortDefinition: The consistency model used between aggregates where state converges over time via domain events rather than locks.
words.simpleDefinition: Eventual consistency is the consistency model that applies between aggregates. When aggregate A changes, it publishes a domain event. Aggregate B reacts to that event in a separate transaction, at some point after A's transaction commits. B's state is not immediately consistent with A's change — it converges to consistency over time. The 'eventually' is usually milliseconds to seconds, not days — but it is not instant.
words.longDefinition: Vernon's Effective Aggregate Design explicitly states Rule 4: use eventual consistency outside the aggregate boundary. This is not a distributed systems compromise — it applies even in a single-process monolith. The aggregate boundary is the unit of transactional commitment regardless of deployment topology. Between aggregates, strong transactional consistency is not possible without coupling the aggregates — and that coupling would undermine the decomposition that makes aggregates valuable as independent consistency units. The mechanism for eventual consistency between aggregates is domain events: when an Order is confirmed, it raises an OrderConfirmed event. The Inventory aggregate handles that event in a separate transaction and decrements its stock. The consistency lag between Order confirmation and Inventory decrement is the 'eventual' window. In a synchronous event handler on the same JVM this window may be microseconds. In an asynchronous message broker with retries it may be seconds. The business must accept this window — and in most domains, it already does. An underwriter signing a policy does not need warehouse stock to decrement atomically in the same second. Eventual consistency also forces explicit failure handling: if the Inventory decrement fails, the system must retry, compensate, or alert — options that are always available with events but hidden by database transaction rollback.
words.connector: Think of eventual consistency like a bank transfer across institutions — your sending bank debits your account immediately, and your receiving bank credits the recipient's account later, after processing. Between the debit and the credit, the total money in both accounts sums correctly — just not at every instant.
words.techContext: After splitting Order and Inventory into separate aggregates, we used eventual consistency via an OrderConfirmed event handled by Inventory — the 200ms consistency window was acceptable to the business and eliminated the lock contention that had been causing order submission timeouts.
words.exampleSentence: The product manager initially objected to eventual consistency between Order and Inventory, until we showed that the warehouse physically could not decrement stock atomically anyway — the system was already eventually consistent; we were just making it explicit.
words.etymology: From database theory — 'eventual consistency' was coined in the distributed systems literature (Werner Vogels, 2009) but Evans applied the concept within a single bounded context to describe the consistency model between aggregates connected by domain events.

words.shortDefinition: The code layer containing entities, value objects, aggregates, and domain services — the heart of a DDD application.
words.simpleDefinition: The domain model layer is where the business lives in code. It contains all the entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, domain services, and repository interfaces that encode the business rules and domain vocabulary. It has zero knowledge of databases, HTTP, queues, or UI frameworks. Everything else in the application is either a delivery mechanism (driving it) or infrastructure (driven by it).
words.longDefinition: In layered architecture terms (Evans, DDD Chapter 4), the domain model layer is the inner ring that all other layers depend on — never the reverse. In hexagonal architecture terms (Cockburn, 2005), the domain model is the hexagon's core, surrounded by ports and adapters. The domain model layer contains: entities (objects with identity that persist through state changes), value objects (immutable objects defined by their attributes), aggregates (consistency clusters with a root gatekeeper), domain services (stateless operations that do not fit on a single entity), domain events (past-tense facts raised when state changes), and repository interfaces (persistence abstractions declared in the domain, implemented in infrastructure). What the domain model layer does NOT contain: SQL queries, ORM annotations, HTTP clients, email senders, file I/O, or framework-specific code. The discipline of keeping these out is what enables the domain model to be unit-tested without spinning up databases or HTTP servers, what enables it to be reused across different delivery mechanisms (REST API and CLI can share the same domain layer), and what preserves the model's integrity over time. When framework code leaks into the domain model — JPA annotations on entity fields, Spring annotations on aggregate methods, HTTP response objects returned from domain services — the domain model begins to model the infrastructure rather than the domain, accelerating model drift.
words.connector: Think of the domain model layer like the engine in a car — it provides the power that makes everything move, but it knows nothing about whether you are driving a sedan or a truck, what color the body is, or who is sitting in the seats. The engine just converts fuel to motion.
words.techContext: When we added a test that instantiated every domain model class without a Spring context, we discovered twelve aggregate methods had accidentally imported Spring annotations — removing them shrunk the domain layer and made it framework-independent.
words.exampleSentence: The code review rule 'no import statements from framework packages inside the domain model layer' caught a developer adding a Hibernate annotation to an entity — keeping the domain model infrastructure-free and testable without a container.
words.etymology: Evans organised DDD around layers — presentation, application, domain, infrastructure — with 'domain model layer' naming the layer whose purpose is purely the expression of domain concepts, isolated from all delivery and storage concerns.

words.shortDefinition: An anti-pattern class that accumulates too many responsibilities by acting as the nearest hook for unrelated logic.
words.simpleDefinition: A god object is a class that has grown to know too much and do too much — it holds global state, coordinates unrelated subsystems, and acts as a catch-all for any logic that does not have a clearer home. In a DDD codebase, god objects typically appear as oversized aggregates or service classes that accumulate every business operation related to a popular entity like Customer or Order.
words.longDefinition: The god object anti-pattern was identified by Riel (Object-Oriented Design Heuristics, 1996) and appears in DDD codebases in two primary forms. The first is the god aggregate: a single aggregate root that grows to contain dozens of entities and hundreds of invariants because it is the natural attach point for every new feature involving that concept. A Customer aggregate that started with contact information, identity, and preferences gradually accumulates order history, loyalty points, subscription status, billing details, and GDPR consent records — none of which require atomic consistency with each other. Loading this aggregate pulls thousands of records; updating it locks a row that concurrent operations compete for constantly. The correct response is to decompose by bounded context and by invariant scope: each cohesive consistency concern belongs in its own appropriately-sized aggregate. The second form is the god service: an application service or domain service that orchestrates so many operations that it functions as a mini-monolith within the codebase. Adding a feature to the god service requires understanding its entire state, producing a change amplification problem. Evans's model-code gap widens fastest around god objects because every developer defaults to attaching new logic to the largest, most visible class rather than introducing a new, appropriately-sized abstraction.
words.connector: Think of a god object like a Swiss Army knife — useful for small tasks, but if your Swiss Army knife has 47 tools including a fishing rod and a pizza oven, it is no longer a knife; it is a liability that nobody can maintain.
words.techContext: Our OrderService had grown to 4,200 lines with 68 public methods spanning fulfilment, billing, notifications, and analytics — decomposing it into four focused services aligned with the corresponding bounded contexts halved average bug-fix time.
words.exampleSentence: The god-object Customer aggregate loaded 47 related tables on every request; decomposing it into three aggregates — Identity, BillingAccount, and LoyaltyProfile — reduced the average load time from 800ms to 12ms.
words.etymology: Named 'god' for the theological concept of an omniscient, omnipotent being — a god object knows everything and does everything, which in software produces the same fragility as concentrating all power in one point.

words.shortDefinition: The breakdown that occurs when a single bounded context serves too many teams, producing ambiguous, competing definitions.
words.simpleDefinition: Model fragmentation happens when a bounded context spans more than one team, or when one context grows so large that different parts of the team use the same word to mean different things. The ubiquitous language breaks down into dialects; the model fragments into competing interpretations; changes to shared concepts ripple unpredictably across features. It is the failure mode of a bounded context that has grown past the capacity of a single team to own.
words.longDefinition: Evans describes model fragmentation in Domain-Driven Design as the natural consequence of letting a model serve too many masters. When one bounded context is written by multiple teams without strict shared ownership, each team introduces their own vocabulary extensions and interprets existing concepts through their own subdomain lens. The word 'Customer' begins meaning something subtly different to the Billing team than to the Fulfilment team, even though they share the same class. Bugs emerge at the intersection of these divergent interpretations — a Billing update to 'Customer.address' that breaks Fulfilment's address validation, because Billing was thinking 'billing address' and Fulfilment was thinking 'shipping address'. Evans's Chapter 14 on context map patterns identifies model fragmentation as the key diagnostic for a context that is too large: symptoms include ambiguous terms that require qualification ('customer in the billing sense'), changes to shared concepts requiring consultation across multiple teams, and the consistent appearance of conflicts in code review that are really disagreements about the domain model. The remedy is context boundary surgery: identify the natural seams where competing definitions arise, draw explicit boundaries at those seams, and assign ownership of each resulting context to one team.
words.connector: Think of model fragmentation like a game of telephone through many players — the original message becomes distorted at each handoff until the version the last player hears bears little resemblance to what the first player said. The only fix is to shorten the chain.
words.techContext: Our single 'Core' bounded context had fragmented to the point where the word 'Account' meant six different things to six different teams — splitting it into Billing, Identity, and Subscription contexts resolved the ambiguity by giving each definition its own clean boundary.
words.exampleSentence: The week-long production incident traced back to model fragmentation: two teams had independently extended the shared 'Order' class in contradictory directions, and a routine deploy from team A silently broke team B's assumptions.
words.etymology: Evans introduced 'model fragmentation' in Domain-Driven Design to name the failure state where a model that was once coherent has split into multiple competing interpretations — 'fragmentation' captures the splintering of a unified language into incompatible dialects.

words.shortDefinition: Repositories speak the domain's aggregate language; DAOs speak SQL rows — the distinction keeps domain models persistence-ignorant.
words.simpleDefinition: A Repository is a domain-level abstraction that works with aggregate objects and uses ubiquitous language method names. A DAO (Data Access Object) is a persistence-level abstraction that maps database rows to simple data structures. The key difference: a repository hides the fact that persistence exists at all; a DAO exposes it as the primary concern. Using DAOs in a DDD domain layer produces anemic domain models because the domain code ends up reasoning about rows rather than aggregates.
words.longDefinition: Evans explicitly distinguishes repositories from DAOs in Domain-Driven Design. A DAO — the J2EE Data Access Object pattern — was designed as a thin layer around JDBC to separate SQL from business code. It maps rows to data transfer objects, exposes table-centric operations (findByTable, insertRow, updateRow), and requires callers to understand the persistence schema. A repository, by contrast, gives the domain layer the illusion that aggregate roots live in an in-memory collection. It exposes operations using the ubiquitous language (findActiveOrdersForCustomer, nextOrderId), returns fully constructed aggregate objects (not rows or DTOs), and hides whether the backing store is Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or an in-memory test double. The practical consequence of confusing them: when application services use DAOs, they take on the responsibility of assembling aggregates from raw row data — which is persistence logic that belongs in the infrastructure layer. The aggregates themselves cannot enforce invariants because they are assembled piecemeal by callers rather than by a single responsible factory-like repository implementation. Repository interfaces belong to the domain layer; DAO implementations belong to the infrastructure layer. A well-designed system might have a DAO inside a repository implementation — the DAO handles the SQL, the repository uses the DAO's results to reconstitute aggregates — but the domain layer only knows about the repository interface.
words.connector: Think of the Repository vs DAO distinction like the difference between a hotel concierge and a room key machine. The concierge (repository) understands what you need as a guest and arranges it in your language. The key machine (DAO) just manages key cards and room numbers — it knows nothing about guests as people.
words.techContext: After replacing direct DAO calls in our application services with repository interfaces, our unit test suite went from requiring a test database to running entirely in-memory — the DAO was an infrastructure concern; the repository was the domain's persistence contract.
words.exampleSentence: The code smell was clear: the application service was calling the OrderDAO, assembling Order objects from three different DTO types, and then checking invariants — logic that belonged entirely inside an OrderRepository implementation.
words.etymology: DAO (Data Access Object) originated in the Sun J2EE Blueprint patterns (1998); Evans deliberately positioned the repository as a domain-level alternative to the DAO, using the collection metaphor to make the distinction conceptually clear.

words.shortDefinition: Application-generated identity strategies that give entities stable IDs without depending on database auto-increment.
words.simpleDefinition: UUIDs and ULIDs are application-generated unique identifiers that an entity can carry from the moment of creation, without waiting for a database to assign an auto-increment key. This persistence-ignorance is critical in DDD: an entity has its identity before it is saved. UUIDs are random 128-bit values; ULIDs are lexicographically sortable 128-bit values that embed a timestamp prefix, giving them time-ordered properties that UUIDs lack.
words.longDefinition: Evans discusses identity generation strategies in Domain-Driven Design (Chapter 5) as a tactical concern with strategic implications. Database-assigned auto-increment IDs couple entity identity to the persistence layer in two harmful ways: first, the entity has no identity until it is saved, which breaks the domain model's ability to reference the entity before persistence; second, the ID generation is a database concern that leaks into the domain model's lifecycle. Application-generated IDs remove both problems. A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier, RFC 4122) is a 128-bit pseudo-random number with negligible collision probability — the entity receives its UUID at construction time, before any database call. A ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) is a 128-bit value with a 48-bit timestamp prefix followed by 80 random bits.
