The timestamp prefix gives ULIDs properties UUIDs lack: ULIDs are naturally ordered by creation time when sorted lexicographically, making them efficient as database primary keys (B-tree indexes remain sorted without page splits) and enabling time-range queries using the ID alone. In DDD practice, wrapping UUID or ULID in a typed value object (OrderID, CustomerID) combines application-generated identity with the type-safety benefits of primitive obsession prevention — the type system prevents passing an OrderID where a CustomerID is expected.
words.connector: Think of UUID/ULID like a social security number assigned at birth rather than one assigned when you first apply for a job — the person has their identity from day one, independent of any external registration system.
words.techContext: Switching from database auto-increment to ULIDs for Order IDs let us create order objects in memory, pass them through domain operations, and batch-insert them without any round-trips to the database to retrieve generated IDs.
words.exampleSentence: The race condition in the order creation flow disappeared after switching to ULIDs: the entity could be fully assembled and validated in memory before the first database call, eliminating the window where a half-created entity had no identity.
words.etymology: UUID stands for Universally Unique Identifier (RFC 4122, 2005); ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) was specified by Alizain Feerasta in 2016 to add sortability to UUID's uniqueness guarantees.

words.shortDefinition: The process of identifying coherent business areas by interviewing domain experts, not by reading the org chart.
words.simpleDefinition: Subdomain discovery is the analytical and collaborative process of identifying the natural partitions of a business domain by talking to domain experts, mapping workflows, and looking for natural seams between coherent business capabilities. It is a discovery activity — subdomains exist in the business whether or not the software recognises them — not a design activity, and the right tool is conversation and observation, not org-chart reading.
words.longDefinition: Evans establishes in Domain-Driven Design that subdomains are discovered in the problem space, not designed in the solution space. The business domain exists independently of any software decisions — its natural partitions are determined by business reality: different vocabularies, different experts, different rate of change, different competitive significance. Subdomain discovery is the practice of uncovering those natural partitions through structured knowledge-crunching sessions. The primary technique is interviewing domain experts and observing where vocabulary shifts, where experts from different disciplines stop understanding each other, and where 'that is not my area' appears in conversation. Those friction points are subdomain boundaries. Secondary techniques include workflow mapping (Event Storming is particularly useful here), competitive analysis (what capabilities make the business unique?), and Conway's Law application (which groups of people work independently without coordination?). Common discovery mistakes include confusing the org chart with the subdomain map (organisational structure often crosses natural domain boundaries), confusing technical modules with business subdomains (a module boundary is a software decision, not a domain fact), and defining subdomains by what the existing software does rather than by what the business actually needs. Subdomain discovery feeds directly into core/supporting/generic classification: once the subdomains are found, the team can assess which provide competitive advantage (core), which are necessary but not differentiating (supporting), and which the market already solves (generic).
words.connector: Think of subdomain discovery like a geologist mapping rock strata — the strata exist in the ground whether or not anyone has mapped them. The geologist's job is to observe, sample, and document the natural layers, not to invent new ones for convenience.
words.techContext: Our three-day subdomain discovery workshop with actuaries, underwriters, and claims adjusters surfaced seven distinct subdomains the engineering team had collapsed into two technical modules — the mismatch explained why every change to 'policy' required coordinating four teams.
words.exampleSentence: The subdomain discovery session revealed that 'customer' meant completely different things to the sales team and the claims team — a discovery that justified splitting what the codebase had treated as one entity into two separate bounded contexts.
words.etymology: Evans introduced 'subdomain discovery' as a deliberate contrast to 'subdomain design' — the word 'discovery' signals that subdomains are found in the business reality, not invented by engineers, and that the process is empirical rather than prescriptive.

words.shortDefinition: The design decision about which objects belong inside one aggregate boundary, driven by invariant scope not convenience.
words.simpleDefinition: Aggregate size is the design decision about which entities and value objects belong together inside a single aggregate boundary. The correct criterion is invariant scope: include only the objects that participate in a business rule that must be enforced atomically. Everything that is merely 'related' but not part of the same invariant belongs outside, referenced by ID, and connected through eventual consistency. Defaulting to large aggregates because objects seem related is the most common aggregate design mistake.
words.longDefinition: Vernon's Effective Aggregate Design (2012) dedicates its central argument to aggregate size, countering the natural instinct to build large aggregates. Large aggregates produce four concrete harms: lock contention (a large aggregate is locked for the duration of its transaction, and the more objects inside, the more concurrent operations compete for that lock), memory pressure (loading a large aggregate forces the entire object graph into memory even when the operation touches one field), invariant ambiguity (large aggregates accumulate many invariants, some of which conflict or become hard to reason about together), and test complexity (large aggregates require extensive setup, making unit tests slow and brittle). Vernon's size heuristics: model only true invariants in the aggregate (include an object only if a business rule spans it and the root), start small and add objects only when an invariant demands it, reference all external aggregates by identity rather than by object, and use eventual consistency wherever the business can tolerate a brief consistency window. The diagnostic question for every object under consideration for aggregate membership is: 'Does a business invariant require this object and the root to be consistent at the same instant?' If the answer is no, the object belongs outside the aggregate. If loading an aggregate requires joining more than a handful of tables, or if concurrent operations produce frequent lock timeouts, the aggregate is almost certainly too large and contains objects that joined it by proximity rather than by invariant necessity.
words.connector: Think of aggregate size like a surgical team — you include only the specialists required for this specific procedure. Inviting the entire hospital staff to an appendectomy does not make the operation better; it creates chaos. Each specialist is present because the procedure genuinely requires their role.
words.techContext: After applying Vernon's size heuristics, our Forum aggregate shrank from including posts, comments, votes, and subscribers down to just the forum metadata and active policies — the rest moved to separate aggregates connected by events, cutting load time by 95%.
words.exampleSentence: The lock timeout investigation revealed the root cause: the BlogPost aggregate included all comments, and a post with 10,000 comments was being locked every time anyone liked the post — splitting comments into their own aggregate eliminated the contention entirely.
words.etymology: Evans discussed aggregate composition in Domain-Driven Design (2003); Vernon made aggregate size an explicit design principle in Effective Aggregate Design (2012), coining the guidance as four numbered rules that practitioners could apply systematically.
